course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
review_basis: Original AIP Module 05 site-ready WebP slides individually inspected from archived source images 01–36; narration explains actual visual flows and comparisons. Renderer verifies live R2 sources.
part_title: Data Preparation, Deployment Modes and Safe Rollouts

scenes.title: Prepare Your Training Data
scenes.narration: In the left column we see several possible sources: datasets in Amazon S3, Athena query output, Amazon EMR processing and Redshift data. The arrows converge on two preparation options. A developer may use notebooks to read, clean and transform data interactively, or a SageMaker Processing job for managed repeatable transformation at scale. Both paths lead to the training-ready dataset on the right. Notice the split into training and validation sets, illustrated by an eighty/twenty example. This prevents us from judging model quality entirely on examples used for learning. In real projects, the split needs to respect time ordering, data leakage and business sampling requirements. The slide's most important lesson is to keep source extraction, cleaning and feature creation separate from the actual training job when repeatability matters. Save the prepared dataset and transformation rules so experiments can be reproduced.

scenes.title: SageMaker Processing Job
scenes.narration: This slide zooms in on the managed processing stage. Source data arrives from S3 on the left, together with optional reference or auxiliary files. A SageMaker Processing job runs a container in the centre. Inside that container, application code cleans records, handles missing values, standardizes formats and creates features. The output area on the right contains a cleaned dataset, a feature dataset and logs or metadata. Trace the arrows carefully: the processing job does not itself train the final prediction model. It produces material that a later training job can consume. Compared with a notebook-only script, this pattern gives an explicit, repeatable processing job with controlled compute resources and durable output. A robust workflow also records the processing image, parameters, input paths and output locations. Those details allow the team to understand exactly which transformation created the data behind a model.

scenes.title: Choose a Deployment Mode
scenes.narration: Three choices are shown side by side. A real-time endpoint remains ready to serve interactive requests and returns a prediction with relatively low latency. Asynchronous inference queues larger or longer-running requests and writes results back to S3 after processing; the client checks or receives completion separately. Batch transform runs predictions over a dataset already stored in S3 and writes another dataset to S3 without maintaining a live endpoint. Look at the examples: web or mobile applications tend to need real-time responses, large-file jobs may fit asynchronous processing, and periodic overnight inference can use batch transform. There is no universally cheapest mode because request volume, instance runtime and latency expectations all matter. Choose the execution pattern according to when requests arrive, how large each payload is, and how quickly the results are needed.

scenes.title: Safe Endpoint Rollout
scenes.narration: This slide shows several techniques to release a new model without immediately directing all production traffic to it. In a blue-green rollout, the current and new model environments coexist during a controlled transition. A canary sends only a small share of requests to the new variant at first. Linear traffic shifting gradually increases that share if health checks remain acceptable. Along the bottom are health monitoring, rollback and shadow testing. Health metrics can include latency, errors and model-quality signals; an automatic rollback can shift traffic back after a predefined degradation alarm. Shadow testing sends copies of requests to a new model without using its responses for normal user decisions, enabling comparison. These mechanisms reduce risk but do not replace compatibility testing or data governance. The goal is to learn from limited exposure and retain a clear path back to the proven model if the release fails.

scenes.title: Build and Train Toolset
scenes.narration: SageMaker Studio is shown in the centre of this diagram as a workspace connecting model-development tools. On the left, notebooks enable exploration and custom code. Across the top, Autopilot can automate supported model-building tasks. Along the bottom, Experiments tracks trial runs and evaluation evidence, Hyperparameter Tuning searches configurations, and Debugger helps inspect supported training issues. The arrows show that these capabilities can be used together, but they do not turn into one mandatory workflow. You might explore in a notebook, track a training experiment, run tuning jobs and then evaluate the best candidate. Another team may use a prebuilt model or a more automated path. The important lesson is to choose tools according to development needs while preserving repeatability. Track which data, code and hyperparameters produced each candidate, then promote only candidates that pass your evaluation requirements.
